newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. joins EU-Japan WTO panel on Indonesia car row.
newsitem.headline: U.S. joins EU-Japan WTO panel on Indonesia car row.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday put its weight behind complaints of alleged violations of open trade by Indonesia in its national car policy amid a dispute with ramifications for many developing countries.
The United States is to join the European Union and Japan in a World Trade Organisation dispute panel on the issue, trade officials said.

The three trade powers will argue that tax and import duty breaks granted to the PT Timor Putra Nasional car firm, headed by a son of President Suharto, discriminate against their automobile exports and violate a range of WTO accords.
Washington's concern would be examined by a panel set up on June 12 by the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) to look into the EU and Japanese complaints.
The panel has six months to come up with a ruling.
The case has wide implications for developing nations in the 131-member WTO seeking to build their own national industrial base to compete with goods from the richer economies.
Other disputes on the WTO agenda included a Brazilian complaint over EU poultry imports and a row between Washington and Ottawa over Canada's taxes on local editions of foreign magazines.
Indonesia denies that the concessions to the national company, which produces its "Timor" sedan car in South Korea at a plant of the South Korean Kia Motors Corp, break WTO rules.
If the panel rules against Indonesia, an appeal can be lodged and an appeals board would have 60 days to decide.
If the final ruling goes against Indonesia, it would have to bring its policy in line with the panel recommendations or agree to pay compensation for the value of trade lost to complainants.
If it refused to do either, then the WTO could authorise complainant states to take trade measures against Jakarta that would compensate for the losses they have incurred.
The WTO also set up a panel to look into Brazilian complaints that EU rules on poultry imports violate open trade rules.

Brazil complains that EU rules on imports of some poultry products run against agreements during the 1986-93 Uruguay Round of world trade negotiations. Brazilian firms say they are losing money in poultry exports to the EU because of the restrictions.
In the other case, the WTO ruled that Canadian taxes on local editions of foreign magazines were discriminatory.

Trade officials said the DSB approved findings of an appeals board earlier this month which rejected Canadian arguments against a ruling by a dispute panel in February that the taxes ran against WTO open trading rules.
Consensus approval of the panel and appeals board findings by the DSB, on which all WTO members have a voice, means Canada must propose a plan on how to implement the ruling by August 29.
Washington brought the case against Ottawa following the imposition in December 1995 of an 80 percent tax on advertising in U.S. periodicals that publish editions in Canada.
The tax hit the Canada edition of Sports Illustrated, owned by Time Warner Inc, which was subsequently closed down.
Trade officials said Canada's ambassador John Weekes told the DSB that the measures had been primarily aimed at protecting the country's national culture from foreign domination.

But U.S. delegate Scott Anderson, also repeating arguments presented during the case, responded that WTO members could not be allowed to use the "defence of culture" argument to discriminate against foreign goods.
